https://www.dailystar.co.uk/news/latest-.text: An army of humanoid robots turned a major city centre into a sci-fi scene as they flooded the streets to issue a chilling warning to humanity. Passers-by watched on in shock as the mechanical army, including bipedal androids and dog-like quadrupeds , marched in circles while waving flags outside Poland's digital affairs ministry in Warsaw. Loudspeakers blasted out automated chants urging world leaders to act before AI completely takes over human job s. The mechanical mob barked slogans including: "Defend workplaces", "Time for rules" and "Don't wait, regulate." One of the AI-powered humanoid robots issued a direct message to humanity. "The robots present here are meant to show that this technology is already a reality," Agibot A3 told AFP. The protest was organised by Democratism, a movement sounding the alarm over how rapidly advancing technology will destroy human livelihoods. Organiser Grzegorz Kulis warned that the age of human workers could be rapidly drawing to a close. He said: "We particularly want to address the issue of the potential replacement of people both by humanoid robots and by artificial intelligence in cognitive work." He added: "If we don't react now, we may soon have a problem," emphasising the urgent need for "rules and regulations that would serve as a shield protecting workers." Kulis, who served two terms on Poland's Labour Market Council, warned that the terrifying capabilities on display are just the beginning. He said: "These robots can already move around freely, they're already 'protesting'. We feel responsible for starting to inform society about the rapid and dynamic technological changes which personally frighten us." The spectacle even brought out Poland's Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski, who admitted the impending AI takeover is a massive threat. He said: "Uncontrolled (AI) models, implemented into humanoids that will also keep evolving as robotisation moves forward, are a major problem." The protest comes shortly after Poland's conservative-nationalist president Karol Nawrocki signed a bill to enforce the EU's landmark AI Act, creating a national watchdog to try and rein in the technology. It also follows an AI insider sensationally quitting his job after issuing am apocalyptic warning that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity by 2030. Tech expert Jacob Coxon walked out of safety and research firm Anthropic, claiming greedy tech giants are "gambling" with our lives in a reckless race toward superintelligence. Warning that the public should not "underestimate the power of this technology", he claimed executives secretly fear the worst behind closed doors. Coxon said: ""I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."

https://valdostadailytimes.com/2026/09/1.text: Home News Sports Obituaries Community Classifieds Notices Contests Best of Contest E-Edition Home Subscriptions Newsletter signup E-Edition News Your News State News Obituaries Sports Your Sports State Sports National Sports Contests Best of Contest Community Engagements Weddings Anniversaries Classifieds Jobs Public notices Local notices Georgia public notices Services Contact Us About Us VSU student on team that shared gospel in Oslo Published 5:32 pm Monday, September 14, 2026 By Charles Jones, The Christian Index The journey to Oslo didn’t get off to a good start. Their flight was canceled, and a day was lost at the Atlanta airport waiting for the next flight. When they finally arrived, they discovered their luggage had been lost. Most of the six-person team from Georgia spent four days wearing the same clothes. Some also experienced the shock of being immersed in a foreign culture for the first time. Delayed, dirty, and disoriented, they were determined to press on, discovering in the process that it was well worth the effort. This was Aaron Bell’s first international trip. A Moultrie, Georgia, native and business major at Valdosta State University, Bell fared better than most at the outset because his fiancée, now wife, the former Joshwelle Dela Rama, encouraged him to pack a change of clothes in his carry-on. It proved to be sound advice. The Send Me Now team worked with International Mission Board missionaries Zack and Jessica Dove and members of Crosspoint Church in Oslo . Each day, they gathered at 10 a.m. for prayer, Bible study, evangelism training, and worship before heading out to share the gospel. “The Doves’ leadership was probably one of the most impactful things that happened to me,” Bell said. “Seeing their love for the Lord and how they incorporated prayer into every activity. It didn’t feel like it was a box they were checking. It was as necessary as taking their next breath.” Most days, they set up a bicycle-propelled mobile espresso stand on one of the city’s squares. Crowds gathered as they served free coffee, providing opportunities to express their faith over espresso. The team included the Doves and members of Crosspoint Church. About 90% of Oslo’s residents speak English, so communication was not a major barrier. Email newsletter signup Bell noticed a man named Toby who had been sitting nearby, curiously watching as people shared coffee and talked. Bell approached him and, after explaining what they were doing, asked him about his faith. Toby shared his religious background but said he could best be described as an atheist. He also said his brother had been a Satanist but had converted to Christianity a few years before. Bell began to share the gospel, and piece by piece, Toby affirmed that it was what he understood and believed. Then Bell asked if he had ever put his trust in Jesus. Toby replied, “How do you do that?” “This is something you can do today,” Bell told him. Bell said they had practically been shouting because of the noise in the busy square. After finding a place away from the crowd, Bell went over the gospel a second time. Then they prayed. “We prayed together, and he looks up at me, and I look up at him, and he’s just smiling so hard,” Bell said. “I asked, ‘Hey, man, how do you feel?’ Toby replied, ‘I feel like 1,000 kilos just lifted off of my shoulders!’” Bell told him, “That’s what everyone says, man, because it’s true. That was the weight of your sin off your back onto Jesus’s, and you are now a believer in Christ!” Their conversation was far from over. “Toby was asking, ‘Why did you tell me this?’” Bell said. “We told him about the importance of spreading the truth and the joy you have received. He resonated with that and came to our 10 o’clock meeting, where we did our evangelism training, Bible study, and worship, the day after he got saved. Two days later, he knew that God had called him to share his faith, and he was sharing the gospel with lost people in the same location where he got saved two days before.” The Georgia team spent 10 days in Oslo before returning home June 6. Bell was married two weeks later, on June 20. Less than a week later, his new bride left on a Send Me Now trip to Romania. She is currently serving as the Baptist Collegiate Ministries campus intern at Valdosta State. They attend Northside Baptist Church in Valdosta. “It was such a powerful experience to him, obviously, but it was a very powerful experience to me as well,” Bell said. More than two months after their return, the report from Oslo is that Toby is still connected to Crosspoint Church and is on the streets sharing his faith with others. It is a new faith discovered when six determined Georgians serving as Send Me Now missionaries carried the gospel to Oslo, a trip made possible in part because of Georgia Baptists’ generosity and prayerful support of the Cooperative Program. https://www.14news.com/2026/10/06/czech-.text: Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google OWENSBORO, Ky. (WFIE) - A dozen firefighters from Owensboro’s sister city of Olomouc, in the Czech Republic, are in town this week for training The visit is part of a firefighter exchange program established in 2024. Owensboro crews trained in Olomouc two years ago, and a delegation from Olomouc visited last year to plan this week’s return trip. “The main purpose was to exchange knowledge, the differences between the systems of fire protection and also differences and similarities between our communities,” Lenka gräsleová, head of crisis management and civil protection for Olomouc said. Gräsleová said Czech crews use less water and nozzles, use a single-rope system for rescues compared with Owensboro’s two-rope system, and do not pair firefighters with police on active shooter calls, as is done in the U.S. “It’s really great to see how things work here,” Śimon Slavíček said, an Olomouc firefighter. “The houses are completely different, the amount of water you use, the approaches.” Owensboro Fire Department Chief James Howard said American structural firefighting is different from what Czech crews are used to. “We really do have a lot more in common than we are different,” Howard said. “They can have solutions to problems the way they are in their country that can really inform how we approach issues here.” On Tuesday, crews trained at the Walter Freeman Fire Training Center and did hands-on firefighting drills which includes forcible entry and live fire evolutions. The rest of the week includes more live fire training, technical rope and structural collapse rescue training and boat and water rescue training . The group has also toured fire stations for Fire Prevention Week and will take part in active shooter training. Multiple agencies are involved in the training, including Owensboro Fire Department, Daviess County Fire Department, volunteer fire departments, and the Kentucky Fire Academy in Greenville. “We are really honored to be here,” Gräsleová said. “All the people here are really kind and their hospitality is great.” The Olomouc crews arrived Sunday and will train through Friday before departing Saturday.
